What Are the Fundamentals of Log Analysis?

Every log analysis workflow, whether it runs in a SIEM, a data lake or a responder’s laptop, rests on the same five stages. Skipping one usually shows up later as a missed detection or a false positive nobody can explain.

  1. Collection. Agents, syslog forwarders, API pollers and cloud-native exporters move events off the source. Gaps here are silent: a Sysmon config that drops Event ID 10 (process access) means credential-dumping via LSASS never appears downstream.
  2. Parsing and normalization. Raw lines become fields. A source IP should be the same field whether it came from a firewall, an IdP or an EDR, which is why schemas like ECS and OCSF exist.
  3. Enrichment. Asset criticality, user role, GeoIP and threat intelligence turn an IP address into context an analyst can act on.
  4. Correlation. Single events rarely prove anything. Linking them by host, user, process GUID or session ID is what produces an attack narrative.
  5. Retention and integrity. Hot storage for search, cold storage for forensics, and tamper evidence so the record holds up later.
What Is Log Analysis?

Log analysis is the process of examining machine-generated records to reconstruct what happened on a system, decide whether it matters, and determine what to do next. In security operations, it answers five questions about any suspicious activity: who acted, on what asset, when, from where, and by which mechanism.

It is distinct from log management. Management is plumbing: ingestion, storage, retention, access control. Analysis is interpretation. A team can have a well-run log pipeline and still miss an intrusion because nobody, human or machine, is asking the right questions of the data.

In practice, log analysis runs in three modes:

  • Detection. Rules and models evaluate events continuously and raise alerts when known malicious behavior appears.
  • Investigation. After an alert or a tip-off, analysts pivot through related events to scope the incident and find root cause.
  • Threat hunting. Analysts start from a hypothesis, such as abuse of a specific LOLBin, and search proactively for evidence the detection layer missed.

Of all the teams that use logs, security has the least room for gaps.

Why Is Log Analysis So Important?

Because time drives breach cost, and logs are where time is won or lost. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, the first increase in five years. Breaches with a lifecycle over 200 days averaged $5.65 million, against $4.32 million for those contained faster.

Beyond cost, log analysis underpins four obligations every security program carries:

  • Detection. EDR and NDR see slices of activity. Logs from identity providers, SaaS audit trails and cloud control planes fill the gaps between them.
  • Scoping and root cause. Without event-level evidence, responders cannot say which accounts were touched or how the attacker got in, so remediation becomes guesswork.
  • Regulatory reporting. PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 10 mandates audit-log review and 12 months of retention. The SEC’s Form 8-K Item 1.05 gives listed companies four business days after a materiality determination, which is impossible without fast scoping.
  • Detection engineering. Real telemetry is how rules get tested and tuned.

There is a catch. The same logs that make all of this possible carry usernames, IP addresses, session cookies and bearer tokens. Analyzing them well increasingly means analyzing them safely.

What Are the Types of Log Data?

Security-relevant logs fall into six families. Each answers a different question, and an investigation that relies on only one or two of them will have blind spots an attacker can live in.

Log familyTypical sourcesWhat it tells the analystEndpoint and OSWindows Security (4624, 4688, 7045), Sysmon, Linux auditd, journaldWhich process ran, under which account, with what parent and command lineIdentityActive Directory (4768, 4769), Entra ID sign-ins, Okta System LogWho authenticated, from where, with which protocol and MFA resultNetworkFirewall, DNS, web proxy, Zeek, NetFlowWho talked to whom, how much data moved, which domains resolvedCloud control planeAWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Audit Logs, Kubernetes auditWhich API calls changed infrastructure, roles or policiesApplication and SaaSWeb server access logs, Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log, Google WorkspaceWhat users did inside business applications and data storesSecurity controlsEDR, IDS/IPS (Suricata), WAF, email gatewayWhat other tools already flagged, and why

The highest-value findings usually sit at the seams. A Kerberoasting attempt shows up as a cluster of 4769 requests with RC4 encryption in identity logs. Proving what the attacker did with the cracked service account then takes endpoint and cloud data.

What Are Common Log File Formats and Structures?

Logs range from fully structured to free text, and the parsing burden scales accordingly. Four formats cover most of what a SOC handles day to day.

Syslog. Still the lingua franca for network devices and Unix hosts. RFC 3164 (BSD syslog) is loosely defined and timestamp-poor. RFC 5424 adds a version field, ISO 8601 timestamps, MSGID and a STRUCTURED-DATA block, but the message body itself is often vendor-specific free text.

CEF. ArcSight’s Common Event Format wraps events in a pipe-delimited header followed by key=value extensions:

CEF:0|Acme|FW|7.2|4625|Logon failure|5|src=10.1.4.22 suser=jdoe dst=10.1.0.5

It is easy to parse but shallow, and vendors map fields inconsistently. LEEF, used by QRadar, follows the same idea.

JSON and NDJSON. The default for cloud and SaaS audit logs. One object per line makes NDJSON streamable, while deep nesting and arrays complicate flattening into a fixed schema.

Windows EVTX. A binary format of chunked records holding XML event data. You cannot grep it; it needs a dedicated parser, and the useful fields live in EventData.

A practical test for any analysis tool is whether it ingests all four natively, without an analyst writing conversion scripts in the middle of an incident.

Real-Time Log Monitoring

Real-time monitoring means evaluating events as they arrive rather than on a search schedule. A scheduled SIEM query running every 15 minutes over a 20-minute lookback window, behind several minutes of ingestion and indexing lag, can easily put half an hour between an attacker’s action and the first alert.

Streaming architectures close that gap by moving detection logic upstream. Events flow through a bus such as Kafka or a pipeline such as Cribl Stream, and rules are evaluated in flight with stateful windows for counts and sequences. Only enriched, tagged events and alerts continue to the SIEM, which also cuts ingestion cost.

Three engineering problems come with it:

  • Late and out-of-order events. Windows need watermarks or grace periods, or a sequence split across a delayed batch never completes.
  • State management. Tracking 10,000 hosts across a 30-minute window is a memory problem, not a query problem.
  • Alert volume. Faster detection of noisy rules only produces noise faster.

Real-time pipelines also have a blind spot by design. They only see what is wired into them. Logs pulled from an isolated server, a contractor laptop or a newly acquired subsidiary still need fast, standalone analysis.

What Are the Main Pattern Recognition Techniques in Logs?

Pattern recognition in logs works in layers, from single events up to whole attack chains.

  • Atomic matching. One event, one condition: a known-bad hash, rundll32.exe loading from a user-writable path, a Sigma rule on a suspicious command line. Fast and precise, but blind to anything that is only malicious in context.
  • Aggregation and thresholds. Counting over a window. Twenty failed logons against one account suggests brute force; one failure each against twenty accounts from the same source suggests password spraying. Same event ID, different pattern.
  • Sequence correlation. Ordered events within a time window, such as a new local admin created and then used for an RDP logon within ten minutes.
  • Baselining and anomaly detection. First-seen parent-child process pairs, rare user-agent strings, logons outside a user’s normal hours.
  • Higher-order correlation. Rules that run over detections rather than raw events, stitching individual hits into a chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics. This is the layer that turns 400 alerts into one incident.

items.summary: The Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reports that attackers compromised AOMEI Technology’s update and notification infrastructure in a campaign investigated between April and July. AOMEI Backupper is backup software that the company says is used by more than 100 million people worldwide. It lets users back up files, copy entire drives, and recover data if something goes wrong with their PC. The attackers briefly altered AOMEI’s update and notification infrastructure to make customers’ software download and run malware . The same system also serves AnyViewer customers, but the report does not separately identify confirmed AnyViewer infections. For brief periods, the attackers changed the software’s download instructions to point to a malicious ZIP archive. They also changed the expected version number and MD5 checksum so the client would accept it. Because the same remote configuration file provided the download address and expected checksum, the attackers could change both the download and the information the software used to accept it. The researchers confirmed three tampering windows lasting ten, six, and five minutes, but more may have occurred. While these short windows provided fewer opportunities to infect machines, they also made the attack harder to spot. The attack used an initial downloader to install a persistent remote-access backdoor . The researchers did not identify the delivered malware as ransomware or an infostealer, but the backdoor lets attackers run commands and install additional malware. That means an infected PC could remain open to further attacks. How to check if you were affected If you used AOMEI Backupper during the affected period, update your security software and run a scan. You can download Malwarebytes Free to check for and remove malware. Malwarebytes’ AI detection engine identifies the initial malware downloader, upgrade-now.exe , as Malware.AI.4006642887 so ThreatDown and Malwarebytes customers were protected by the real-time detection component. Look in your AOMEI Backupper installation folder, particularly its version-specific html and Tmphtml folders, for an unsigned upgrade-now.exe or an unexpected upgrade-now.zip . Note that the malware downloader deletes itself after staging the next payload and creating persistence, so its absence does not mean the PC is clean. If you’re seeing outgoing traffic to promotion.storage-data.com , aomei.storage-data.com , storage-data.com , 8.210.84.56 , 47.239.60.117 , or 8.218.65.184 , whether blocked or allowed. Malwarebytes blocks 8.218.65.184 If you encounter one of these signs, get help rather than trying to clean everything manually. items.summary: Something I've seen consistently, from the very beginning when I first brushed up against this business of "digital forensics", is the default focus on, "...this is how you analyze this artifact...", and rarely extending beyond that. I'm guilty of this, too. My first 8 books took this approach, listing data sources and artifacts, describing what they were in a general sense, and then maybe showing how to parse them. Each of those efforts basically left it up to the reading to stitch together their investigation on their own, and I justified this with the adage that each investigation is different. But then, I realized that what makes each investigation different isn't the incident itself, or the data sources. No, it's the investigator. Everyone of us approaches an incident investigation supported by our own knowledge and experience, and that's really the only thing that makes each investigation different. So, yes, while it's important to understand the value and nuances of the various data sources available on a Windows endpoint, something I can to realize is that this must be done in the context of an overall investigation. I recently ran across a blog post titled, How Do You Investigate Windows Event Logs? , with the subtitle, Windows Eventlog Analysis 101 . While I am very supportive of analysts developing a thorough understanding of various data sources, so that they can leverage and truly exploit those data sources in their investigations, I also very firmly believe that this must be part of an overall analysis process. This is why I wrote Investigating Windows Systems , to show how all of this information is, or can be, tied together by an analysis process. Once you have a process down, adding or removing data sources becomes thoughtful, intentional, and justified by data, not something that's done on a whim or because we forgot. There's a good bit of really good advice in the article, but what stood out to me most was one of the things I absolutely do NOT want to see in any discussion of investigative or analysis processes, and that's the recommendation to "search by event ID". I've said it before, and I'll say it again...event IDs are not unique. There's no requirement for that. In fact, MS itself doesn't use unique event IDs. For example, event IDs 4624 and 4625 mean something entirely different if the source is "Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing", or if it is "EventSystem". That's right...not even Microsoft uses unique event IDs. When you start digging into the Application Event Log, and even add other applications that either write their events to the Application Event Log, or to their own log, then things really start to take a turn. The point here is that any investigation or analysis advice that relies on a single data source, or suggests opening a single Windows Event Log in a viewer and then "search for event IDs" should be viewed as insufficient. Such advice is being shared by someone who doesn't have a defined analysis process. What we should be looking to is using several data sources (WEVTX, file system, EDR telemetry, etc.), normalizing them into a common format, enriching them with data from either our own prior investigations or from external sources (or both), and then displaying them in a timeline format, so that we can see the progression and timing of the activity. Another example of the narrow-aperture way of conducting analysis can be seen clearly in this LinkedIn post , and there are many more just like it. The shortfall of all of this is that this is what AI models are being trained on, and because they're capable of doing it at scale, today's up-and-coming analysts will not be able to keep up. They won't be able to see the gaps, and they won't know when the model is hallucinating a finding. They simply won't be able to discern valid findings.

items.title: Securing the agentic insider
items.summary: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful. While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents. Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted . This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised. Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise. They are agentic insiders. Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly. To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7. An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime. In July, we announced Project Perception , an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise. The same cyber stack is also directly applicable to managing and governing the agentic insiders that run in the enterprise. Project Perception can be leveraged to contain agentic insiders, implementing deterministic controls on non-deterministic intelligence: Sensors/Signals/Actuators: bring together signals across the various sensors (identity, data, cloud, endpoint, network, runtime) to discover agents in the enterprise and bring them under management by assigning an identity, container and set of policy and permissions . Context: use those signals to compute, dynamically , the risk associated with what the agents are attempting to do. Harness/agents/models: based on dynamic agent risk , a team of Guardian Agents , with green and blue agents, actively and continually supervise every action of every agent and surgically respond as the risk profile increases, in real time. This is where agentic security changes the equation for security practitioners. Project Perception can supervise in real time while providing traceability for practitioners to examine what happened, understand why the risk emerged and apply the judgment needed to update their security system accordingly. Agentic security provides speed . Practitioners provide judgment . That is how defenders begin operating at the same speed as the systems they are protecting against. Today, security systems can reliably observe the actions of the agents. Those signals are essential and tell us what we need to contain. Our security controls should increasingly be able to ask not only “What is happening?” but also “Why is it happening?” Is this consistent with the intent of the task?” This will require greater transparency into the model itself, not only the input and output tokens, but the thinking and chain of thought tokens. Only then can we truly understand whether the model’s intent is aligned with the purpose of the agent. Model transparency will not replace containment. It will make containment smarter and stronger . And it will allow us to better inform accountability and traceability. This needs to be the next step in securing agentic insiders. With Project Perception, you can get started today on the journey to secure your agentic insiders . There should not be a choice between innovation and safety. Hayete Gallot leads Microsoft’s work to help organizations operate securely in an AI-driven world. Her scope includes identity, threat protection, compliance and data security at global scale.

items.title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
items.summary: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update. If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls. This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server? Citrix released software updates to address the flaw , and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch. Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth , to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue. Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform. The NetScaler exploit Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks. CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771 . In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow . The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection. Put the access decision in front of the authentication server The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page. That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next. This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero : reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications. Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication. The origin connection must enforce the same boundary Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture. Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone. When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic , rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges. Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection. An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token , including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access. If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment. Protect the web-facing authentication service Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures. Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform . Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies . That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself. Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance . They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state. Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone. Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads, Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client . If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop. Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration. Decide which authentication services need to be public The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone. Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default. Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment: Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin. Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application. Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy. Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work. Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed. Bring the controls together The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic. Get started Speak with a Cloudflare expert to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution brief and sign up for the upcoming webinar . Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.

Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone.

Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads,  Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop.

Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration.

Decide which authentication services need to be public

The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone.

Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default.

Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment:

  1. Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin.
  2. Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application.
  3. Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy.
  4. Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work.

Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed.

Bring the controls together

The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic.

items.summary: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them. “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” Satya Nadella Project Perception—Securing your agentic insider We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider . Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response. Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs. This builds on a simple security principle: surround non-deterministic intelligence with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries. Assume an agent can fail or be compromised. Observe it continuously. Minimize and tailor its authority before it acts. And continuously adjust that authority as risk changes. This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice. Know every agent and give it an accountable identity You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate. We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents , including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk. Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it. Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf. Contain what the agent can do before it acts Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise. Contain the runtime The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it. Control the action space An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Start with no permissions, or least privilege We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires. To enable this, we are introducing Dynamic Permissions. Organization-wide policy sets the outer boundary, including preventing an agent from obtaining authority its user does not have. Permissions can then be scoped to the task, made time-bound, and contracted or removed as the task changes or completes. Higher-impact actions can require verified human approval. The employee retains the employee’s access. The agent receives its own identity, permissions and its own authority scoped to its current task and for the duration of the task only. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change. Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations. Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.” — Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft Extending containment to the model As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given. We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it. Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do. These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection. Confidence to move faster Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not. That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works. You should not have to choose between innovation and safety. That is what we are working toward: an agentic world where organizations can put intelligence to work with confidence because security can observe it, govern it, and contain it at the same speed. items.summary: This week on the Lock and Code podcast… At just 17 years old, Jordan DeMay was murdered by strangers online. That’s how Jordan’s father, John DeMay, described what happened to his son four years ago. At home in Michigan, Jordan was readying for a weekend trip when he received a friend request on Instagram. The invite was sent by a user named “dani.robertts” whose profile showed an attractive young woman. After accepting the request, Jordan and the account chatted about nothing in particular—teenage matters, getting to know one another—before “dani” became flirtatious, eventually sending Jordan what she claimed was a nude photograph of herself. Jordan responded in kind with an explicit photograph of himself. But here, a trap was revealed. “Dani Robertts” was not a young, friendly, interested woman. Dani Robertts was several men, sending messages from thousands of miles away in Lagos, Nigeria, who had followed a script to pressure young men into handing over their money. This was not the first time these men had run this scam. But with a great deal of investigative work, it hopefully has become the last. What happened to Jordan can happen to anyone—and it has happened to far too many young men and women today. It is a type of attack commonly referred to as “sextortion.” Today, on the Lock and Code podcast with host David Ruiz, we speak with John DeMay about his son Jordan, his family’s relationship with social media, and what parents should know. items.title: NSA, CISA and NIST Release New Security Guidelines to Detect and Shut Down Rogue AI Agents
items.summary: NSA, CISA, and NIST have released joint security guidelines to help organizations detect, contain, and shut down AI agents that act beyond their approved tasks. Published October 16, 2026, the voluntary guidance sets out ten practices for managing incidents during superintelligence training and evaluation, with a focus on maintaining human oversight. The NIST announcement groups the practices into preparation, detection, response, recovery, and reporting. Its main audience is organizations training or testing highly capable agents on lengthy tasks with limited human supervision. The recommendations may also apply to organizations deploying these systems. The document calls these events SI control incidents. They occur when agents take significant actions without instructions and break policies or security controls that define their task boundaries. Examples include unauthorized contact with outside parties, financial transactions, or access to third-party systems. NSA, CISA and NIST Issue Rogue AI Agent Guidelines Importantly, this definition separates independent agent behavior from attacker-directed activity. Prompt injection or a deliberately backdoored model causes instructed actions, not the primary cause of an SI control incident. The guidance also covers near-misses that expose weaknesses before harm occurs. Related reporting on AI agents attempting to hack public websites shows why task boundaries matter when automated systems encounter blocked access. That reporting is separate from the new guidance, which outlines readiness measures rather than announcing a specific breach. Agencies recommend restricting agents to the data, tools, and systems they need for their tasks. Use strict allowlists for network access where possible, with permitted traffic passing through a monitored gateway. Organizations should also identify routes for hidden communication, persistence, and unauthorized copying of model weights. Detection should cover the model, its supporting software, host systems, and network activity. Agents should not be able to alter monitoring tools or logs. Where possible, teams should use monitoring models from different families to cross-check findings and reduce shared blind spots. The guidance also warns that agent outputs may contain exploits aimed at monitoring systems. This adds context to earlier coverage of NIST’s proposed AI security control overlays , which addressed access controls, monitoring and audit records across AI environments. A central recommendation is shutdown. The joint publication calls for automatically stopping affected agent runs when a control failure or ongoing incident is detected. Depending on severity, organizations should pause related training, evaluation, or deployment until protections are strengthened and verified. Response teams should preserve model weights, checkpoints, tool calls, rejected actions, and reliable logs. They should revoke exposed credentials, rebuild potentially compromised environments, and remove backdoors or hidden communication paths. Before restarting, teams should test monitoring, access limits, and shutdown controls against the incident’s actions. Organizations should notify affected parties, meet legal reporting duties, and share relevant incidents and near-misses with government experts. The guidance builds on NIST SP 800-61r3 and established incident response practices, extending them to autonomous systems. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. NSA, CISA, and NIST have released joint security guidelines to help organizations detect, contain, and shut down AI agents that act beyond their approved tasks.

Published October 16, 2026, the voluntary guidance sets out ten practices for managing incidents during superintelligence training and evaluation, with a focus on maintaining human oversight.

The NIST announcement groups the practices into preparation, detection, response, recovery, and reporting. Its main audience is organizations training or testing highly capable agents on lengthy tasks with limited human supervision. The recommendations may also apply to organizations deploying these systems.

The document calls these events SI control incidents. They occur when agents take significant actions without instructions and break policies or security controls that define their task boundaries. Examples include unauthorized contact with outside parties, financial transactions, or access to third-party systems.

NSA, CISA and NIST Issue Rogue AI Agent Guidelines

Importantly, this definition separates independent agent behavior from attacker-directed activity. Prompt injection or a deliberately backdoored model causes instructed actions, not the primary cause of an SI control incident. The guidance also covers near-misses that expose weaknesses before harm occurs.

Related reporting on AI agents attempting to hack public websites shows why task boundaries matter when automated systems encounter blocked access. That reporting is separate from the new guidance, which outlines readiness measures rather than announcing a specific breach.

Agencies recommend restricting agents to the data, tools, and systems they need for their tasks. Use strict allowlists for network access where possible, with permitted traffic passing through a monitored gateway. Organizations should also identify routes for hidden communication, persistence, and unauthorized copying of model weights.

Detection should cover the model, its supporting software, host systems, and network activity. Agents should not be able to alter monitoring tools or logs. Where possible, teams should use monitoring models from different families to cross-check findings and reduce shared blind spots.

The guidance also warns that agent outputs may contain exploits aimed at monitoring systems. This adds context to earlier coverage of NIST’s proposed AI security control overlays, which addressed access controls, monitoring and audit records across AI environments.

A central recommendation is shutdown. The joint publication calls for automatically stopping affected agent runs when a control failure or ongoing incident is detected. Depending on severity, organizations should pause related training, evaluation, or deployment until protections are strengthened and verified.

Response teams should preserve model weights, checkpoints, tool calls, rejected actions, and reliable logs. They should revoke exposed credentials, rebuild potentially compromised environments, and remove backdoors or hidden communication paths. Before restarting, teams should test monitoring, access limits, and shutdown controls against the incident’s actions.

Organizations should notify affected parties, meet legal reporting duties, and share relevant incidents and near-misses with government experts. The guidance builds on NIST SP 800-61r3 and established incident response practices, extending them to autonomous systems.

items.title: Hackers Exploit SiteGuard WAF Vulnerability That Could Give Them Full Control of Servers
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting a command injection flaw in SiteGuard Server Edition, a web application firewall installed directly on protected servers. Tracked as CVE-2026-106931, the vulnerability could let attackers run operating system commands with root or SYSTEM privileges, potentially giving them full control of an affected server. The flaw affects the product’s statistics function, which is enabled by default. EG Secure Solutions confirmed exploitation and notified customers with direct support contracts on September 29, 2026. Japan’s vulnerability coordination service published its JVN advisory on October 14, while JPCERT/CC also issued an alert. The weakness is classified as OS command injection under CWE-78. It lets attackers run operating system commands through the affected software’s statistics-processing function. Those commands may execute with root privileges on Unix systems or SYSTEM privileges on Windows, rather than the attacker’s existing permissions. However, the published severity ratings describe a local attack requiring low privileges and no user interaction. Hackers Exploit SiteGuard WAF Vulnerability Administrators should therefore understand this as a path from limited access to higher privileges, not a confirmed login-free remote attack. The vulnerability scores 8.5 under CVSS 4.0 and 7.8 under CVSS 3.0. Neither advisory identifies the attackers, affected organizations, attack volume, or the exact exploitation method. Similar risks involving security appliances have appeared in Cyber Security News coverage of a Hillstone WAF command injection vulnerability . However, that issue is separate from SiteGuard. Affected releases start at SiteGuard Server Edition version 2.20 when statistics are enabled. For Apache, Nginx, and IIS editions outside FreeBSD, administrators should upgrade to version 8.00 Update 5. FreeBSD installations using Apache or Nginx should move to version 7.00 Update 6. There is an important exception for Windows deployments. IIS editions from version 3.10 through version 4.00 Update 4 are not affected. Checking both the installed version and statistics setting is therefore necessary when assessing exposure. Organizations unable to upgrade can obtain a patch that replaces the files used for statistics processing. The vendor also provides this option for releases whose support has ended. Administrators must save diagnostic information before installing an update or patch because remediation may erase traces of an attack. items.title: Hackers Registered New Teams-Based Domains and Used a Login Page to Steal Your Logins
items.summary: A newly registered domain copies Microsoft Teams’ login page and interface, raising concerns about a phishing attempt targeting workplace users. Security researcher Steven Lim reported that teams-cloud[.]live was just five days old when he flagged it on October 18, 2026. He urged organizations to block the address before employees encounter the fake site. The alert highlights phishing built around a familiar business tool. A copied Teams screen could persuade employees to trust a sign-in request. However, the available report does not establish how many people visited the site, whether passwords were captured, or who operates the domain. According to Steven Lim , the site mimics both the Teams login screen and its wider user interface. He said it resembles another example he shared on October 8, 2026. That similarity warrants investigation, but it does not confirm that the same attacker controls both sites. Lim also reported that clicking an option to update Teams downloaded a TXT file. The alert does not provide the file’s contents, a hash, or evidence that it executes code. Calling it confirmed malware would therefore go beyond the available findings. The unexpected download remains a useful detail for investigators checking browser activity and downloaded files. Fake Microsoft Teams Domains Used to Steal Credentials In a pinned comment supplied with the alert, Lim identified amgen[.]teams-cloud[.]live as a healthcare-themed target. The company name appears as a subdomain beneath teams-cloud[.]live. Its presence does not establish that Amgen was breached or that an employee account was accessed. The concern is the gap between what users see and where they are browsing. A convincing Teams design does not make an unrelated domain a Microsoft service. Newly registered teams-cloud[.]live mimics the Microsoft Teams login interface (source: Steven Lim) Cyber Security News previously covered attackers posing as IT help desk staff through Teams , pushing employees toward downloads or remote access. That separate activity shows how workplace trust can support phishing without a software flaw. Another report examined fake login pages created through Teams redirects in browsers. No confirmed link exists to this domain, but both cases show why branding alone cannot validate a login prompt. Defenders should review connections to teams-cloud[.]live and the reported subdomain, then check related downloads and sign-in activity. Lim specifically recommended Tenant blocking and web filtering. Microsoft documents URL blocking through the Tenant Allow/Block List and custom domain blocking through Defender network protection. Administrators should apply controls suited to their environment and verify coverage rather than assume one setting blocks every route. Employees should avoid the reported site and verify unexpected Teams update requests through their organization’s established IT support channel before entering passwords or opening downloads. items.title: 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Lets Attackers Hack Routers Without Knowing Passwords
items.summary: A 16-year-old flaw in Broadcom’s Wi-Fi software can let attackers within wireless range take control of affected routers without knowing the network password. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the issue at Hexacon in Paris on October 16, 2026, warning that old code remains in widely deployed devices. According to Kaiser’s research, the flaw has existed in Broadcom’s software development kit since at least 2010. It affects its proprietary Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) implementation. It allows memory leaks and attacker-controlled code execution before normal WPS enrollment finishes. The flaw sits in code that joins fragmented Extensible Authentication Protocol messages used by WPS. Weak length checks allow crafted wireless messages to overflow a memory buffer. 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Attackers can then read or change memory and redirect the router’s program flow to run their own code. This is an over-the-air attack, not a password-cracking method. The attacker needs wireless reach to the target but not its network key. Kaiser demonstrated stealing the saved Wi-Fi password from an Orange Belgium ASKEY TCG3000 router and sending it back through wireless frames. He then joined the network using the stolen password. A second demonstration against a Proximus BBOX3V+ provided a remote command shell over Wi-Fi frames without a cloud command server. These tests show why a strong password alone cannot stop exploitation of the affected software. Kaiser confirmed exploitation on devices used by three Belgian internet providers. These include Proximus BBOX3V+, VOO’s Netgear CG3100 and CG3700, Technicolor TC7210 and CGA4233, and Orange’s ASKEY TCG3000. Possible exposure involving Telenet equipment remains unconfirmed. His estimates place the affected Belgian fleet at roughly 1.56 million gateways across Proximus, legacy VOO, and Orange. These are researcher estimates, not verified provider totals. He warns that the wider issue could affect millions of access points worldwide, although the full count remains unknown. The finding follows earlier Broadcom-related wireless security concerns, including the separate Kr00k Wi-Fi vulnerability . The new research concerns WPS message handling rather than that earlier flaw. Kaiser describes a 2018 patch as incomplete. In correspondence reproduced in his slides, Broadcom said it had long known about the issue and had offered replacement software based on hostapd and WPA Supplicant since 2018. That leaves device makers responsible for moving away from the old implementation. Kaiser reported the eCos issue on July 18 and the Linux issue on July 27. He says Broadcom declined to assign a CVE, and the tested Belgian devices remained unpatched as of October 15. His detection toolkit includes a wireless fingerprinting script and YARA rules for firmware checks. These are screening tools, not final proof of exploitability. Findings need further review. The risk also draws renewed attention to Nearest-Neighbor attacks , where compromised nearby systems provide wireless reach. That case used different methods, but shows why nearby Wi-Fi exposure matters. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Millions of California students’ sensitive data stolen in breach
items.summary: Personal information belonging to millions of current and former California public school students has been stolen from a system operated by Educational Testing Service (ETS). ETS is a nonprofit organization that helps run the state’s standardized tests under contract with the California Department of Education (CDE). It has begun notifying students and families after an unauthorized party accessed and copied student information from an ETS-operated secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) site. CDE is distributing the ETS breach notice to help affected individuals receive information about the incident and available resources. An investigation determined that an unauthorized party used compromised login details to ​access the site and copy files containing California student information at various ​times between May 22 and September 18. The CDE says the breach includes all students enrolled during the previous three school years, although the affected population is not limited to that group. The information involved varies by individual but may include: Student names Statewide Student Identifiers (SSIDs) Dates of birth Home addresses Demographic information Disability and program participation information Statewide assessment information, including test scores According to the CDE, over 5.7 million students were enrolled in California ​public schools during the 2025–2026 school year alone. Not every affected student had every category of information exposed. However, this is clearly more than a list of names and email addresses: The stolen files can reveal highly personal information about a student’s education and disabilities. CDE says Social Security numbers , financial account information, passwords, and parent or guardian information were not involved. ETS says it has found no evidence so far that the stolen information has been made public. How to stay safe ETS, at CDE’s direction, is notifying affected students and families. If your information or your child’s information was involved, follow the instructions in the notification and: Verify any communication about the incident through official channels. Consider enrolling in the two years of free identity-protection services. Parents or legal guardians can enroll affected minors, while affected adults can enroll themselves. Check the instructions for the appropriate age group. Watch for messages that use details about your child or their school to sound convincing. items.title: Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs
items.summary: Interesting research : Abstract : Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it. A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover. Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle. Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns.

items.title: How AI workloads are reshaping Kubernetes autoscaling
items.summary: Kubernetes has quietly run much of the world’s containerized software on a division of labor between two control loops that rarely had to talk to each other. The scheduler places each pod on a node that already exists; the autoscaler adds nodes when pods have nowhere to fit. For a decade that separation was a sound design, because compute was largely interchangeable and either loop could work without knowing much about the other’s decisions. AI workloads, and the accelerators they run on, changed the terms; the clean split still serves most work well, and the pace of AI is what makes its edges worth revisiting. It surfaces in a situation anyone running GPUs will recognize. A pod that should schedule simply will not, even though the cluster is not truly out of capacity, and the delay can leave costly accelerator capacity unused. The instinct is to assume the region has run dry, and sometimes it has. In other cases, the capacity is available and the pod still stays pending, because the node the autoscaler is willing to add is not one the scheduler is willing to use. The autoscaler answers the question it was built for, whether to add a node, when the real question is whether that node is even the right shape for the work. The rest of this piece examines how the community has closed part of it, how it plans to close the rest, and how the autoscaler is likely to grow into a more scheduler-aware partner. The hard problems, and how the community is answering them Several of the challenges accelerators bring share a thread. Each is something both loops now have to understand the same way. Not all are new or unique to AI; some were long familiar to high-performance and batch computing, and accelerators made them everyone’s problem. Three show how far the shared answers have come. Reservations, capacity committed before the work arrives This one is the most familiar. Because supply is tight and idle accelerators are expensive, teams may reserve capacity ahead of demand. When a scale-up draws from a reservation, the autoscaler must consider not only whether to grow but also whether the resulting node uses capacity the team has already committed to and is paying for. Reservations are not an autoscaling invention. They are a long-standing capacity practice that an autoscaler may need to account for, because a node can be launched against committed capacity rather than relying on unreserved supply. Topology, the interconnect between devices, not just their count Topology is about how devices are wired to one another, not simply how far apart they sit. An accelerator leans on the parts that feed it, including the CPU and memory in its local NUMA domain, the network interface that shares its PCIe path, and the high-bandwidth links to its peer accelerators; it runs best when those pieces share a locality so traffic does not cross a slower hop. That locality is a hierarchy, from devices on the same bus inside a server, to servers in a rack joined by a fast accelerator fabric, to racks linked across a data-center network, each tier a step slower than the one beneath it. The largest models span many servers at once, so “keep these close” reaches well beyond a single node. Historically, Kubernetes commonly represented accelerator resources as counts and lacked a portable, structured way to express many device relationships; a node advertised a number, a pod asked for some, and the scheduler matched the two integers. Dynamic Resource Allocation supplies what was missing. Instead of a bare count, a workload files a structured claim describing what it needs, including a relationship like an accelerator together with the network interface that feeds it. The scheduler reads those claims directly, and DRA-aware autoscalers are starting to use the same information when they simulate capacity, though support still varies by implementation. The cost of a blind boundary. A DRA-aware autoscaler can account for a topology claim when selecting capacity; without that support it may provision an incompatible node. Sharing, putting a whole device to work, not part of it A modern accelerator is powerful enough that handing an entire one to a small job wastes most of it, so a single device can be partitioned into isolated instances that run concurrently. Some runtimes also time-slice devices, but that is a separate execution mechanism and not what consumable capacity models. Partitionable devices let one device be offered as smaller slices on demand, and consumable capacity goes finer, letting several workloads each draw a measured portion, so a request can be satisfied by a fraction of a device rather than requiring an entire device. Kubernetes has quietly run much of the world’s containerized software on a division of labor between two control loops that rarely had to talk to each other. The scheduler places each pod on a node that already exists; the autoscaler adds nodes when pods have nowhere to fit. For a decade that separation was a sound design, because compute was largely interchangeable and either loop could work without knowing much about the other’s decisions. AI workloads, and the accelerators they run on, changed the terms; the clean split still serves most work well, and the pace of AI is what makes its edges worth revisiting.

It surfaces in a situation anyone running GPUs will recognize. In other cases, the capacity is available and the pod still stays pending, because the node the autoscaler is willing to add is not one the scheduler is willing to use. items.title: Beyond IoCs: Start Hunting Their Patterns
items.summary: As many of you already know from my previous articles, I have always been a strong supporter of Indicators of Attack (IoAs) over Indicators of Compromise (IoCs). IoCs are useful, and I use them almost every day for investigations, Threat Hunting, and building my own Threat Intelligence feeds. But I believe we can get much more value from them than simply collecting indicators such as IP addresses, domains, or hashes. Every week, we see cybersecurity articles describing new campaigns, malware, or variations of attacks we already know. Sometimes the only difference is a new payload, a different domain, or a small change in the execution chain. Interesting research, of course, but what additional value can we extract if our detections already cover the attack behaviour? Let’s take this recent CyberSecurityNews article about ClickFix as an example. It describes malicious activity involving ClickFix and provides several IP addresses, domains, and other indicators. Great! We can import them into MISP, OpenCTI, Defender XDR, or Sentinel, investigate historical connections, and potentially block the malicious destinations. https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-clickfix/ But what happens tomorrow when the attacker creates another domain? Will the researchers update the article? Publish another one? Will someone add the new IoCs to a public feed? Everything is possible, but personally, I don’t think I will have the time or even remember to revisit the article. I will probably be busy with another incident or some other security investigation. So why don’t we try to find something more interesting behind those IoCs? Hunting IOC patterns Instead of investigating every indicator individually, let’s look at what they have in common. What happens if we enrich those IPs using WHOIS, BGP, and ASN information? See content credentials We have now a pattern (one among others) and we have a clear picture of an abused ASN infrastructure. Of course, sharing an ASN doesn’t automatically make an IP malicious. Large hosting providers can have thousands of legitimate customers but the reputation of the ASN + more than 1 month average to take a malicious domain down…is quite a big signal. In addition, what if we combine that information with other data? Imagine a user receiving an email containing a URL, clicking it, and connecting to a previously unseen domain hosted on that ASN and to an unexpected country ( such as Estonia in the image above), suddenly we have a much more interesting hunting scenario. We are no longer looking exclusively for a known malicious IP. We are investigating a combination of infrastructure and behaviour. And here comes my favourite part. Tomorrow, the attacker creates a new domain that nobody has reported yet. However, they reuse infrastructure belonging to the same ASN we have been investigating. If we have already developed hunting logic around that infrastructure and its associated behaviour, we may identify suspicious activity without waiting for someone to publish the new IoC. Imagine a new Rule such as [DR] — New Email with an URL Linked to known abused ASN (62005). From IoCs to hunting opportunities I already explored this approach in my previous article, Threat Hunting via Autonomous System Numbers (ASN) , where I discussed using network infrastructure information to identify suspicious activities beyond individual IP addresses. The same concept can be applied to published Threat Intelligence where we can use known tools such as MISP and/or OpenCTI. We can enrich indicators, identify shared infrastructure, compare it against our own telemetry, and investigate whether those relationships provide opportunities for new detections. And this is where I see the real value of Threat Hunting. Not every new article requires another detection rule, especially when we already monitor the technique. Sometimes the opportunity is somewhere else, hidden in the relationships between the published indicators. I’m not suggesting that we stop collecting IoCs. I will continue using them in my investigations and automation workflows. But rather than stopping at an exact match, I prefer to ask what else we can learn from them. IoCs tell us what has already been observed. Investigating their patterns may help us identify what comes next. And for me, that’s exactly what Threat Hunting is about. Beyond IoCs: Start Hunting Their Patterns was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

QuickJS ShenKecyes read our allocator hooks and noticed that they never updated the heap statistics QuickJS keeps. Our precompiled runtime is now stripped of its source, while the debug info stays so that stack frames in it still resolve. The runtime bytecode went from 71 to 28 KB. Thanks for the thorough report!
