items.summary_html:
Fallout from the QuickJS rebase, found by @ShenKecyes, a V8 fix for pointer authentication by @hsorbo, and better iOS device discovery on Linux.

QuickJS

ShenKecyes read our allocator hooks and noticed that they never updated the heap statistics QuickJS keeps. QuickJS decides when to collect cycles based on the amount of memory allocated, so with that counter stuck at zero, cyclic garbage lived until an explicit gc(). The hooks now track usage, and collection kicks in on its own again.

They also spotted that current QuickJS keeps the source along with the bytecode by default, which the old version never did. Our precompiled runtime is now stripped of its source, while the debug info stays so that stack frames in it still resolve. The runtime bytecode went from 71 to 28 KB. Thanks for the thorough report!

Along the way I found that QuickJS finalizers are per class, and only the base Sampler had one, so every sampler created from JS leaked. A CallCountSampler thus stayed attached after unload, and a later Stalker test following a thread through the stale hook deadlocked on the allocator lock.

V8 on arm64e

Håvard tracked down a fault in the first garbage collection that scanned the stack, in processes using pointer authentication. V8’s register-pushing stack walker calls its callback through a plain BLR, but the callback arrives as a C function pointer signed with the IA key, so the branch landed on the signed value. It now branches through BLRAAZ when the host authenticates pointers. Thanks!

iOS devices on Linux

Discovering an iOS device over the network on Linux relied on systemd-resolved for mDNS browsing. Where it isn’t running, or has multicast DNS turned off, we now fall back to Avahi over D-Bus, resolving the pairing service the same way. And if the mDNS reply never arrives, the timeout error now suggests that a netfilter rule may be dropping it, as that is what it usually turns out to be.

Two XPC fixes came out of the same session. Replies larger than the HTTP/2 window stalled, as only the connection-level window was replenished and never the stream’s. And double and date objects are now decoded instead of being rejected.

macOS

Our OpenSSL-backed glib-networking crashed on every macOS trust store lookup. Mistakes were made when porting our existing patch to the new glib-networking: two of the Security framework constants it looked up are CFSTR() macros rather than exported symbols, so dlsym() returned NULL. They are now created as strings.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • gumjs: Track QuickJS heap usage in the allocator hooks, so cycles are collected without an explicit gc(). Thanks @ShenKecyes!
  • gumjs: Strip the source from the QuickJS runtime bytecode, keeping debug info, shrinking it from 71 to 28 KB. Thanks @ShenKecyes!
  • gumjs: Finalize QuickJS sampler subclasses, fixing a leak that kept samplers attached after unload.
  • v8: Authenticate the stack scan callback on arm64e. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • fruity: Fall back to Avahi for mDNS browsing when systemd-resolved isn’t available or has multicast DNS disabled.
  • fruity: Suggest a firewall rule as the cause when an mDNS reply times out.
  • fruity: Fix XPC flow control for replies larger than the HTTP/2 window.
  • fruity: Decode double and date XPC objects.
  • glib-networking: Fix the macOS trust store lookup, which crashed since the last SDK bump.

items.title: ShinyHunters Exploits Oracle PeopleSoft to Steal Sensitive Data
items.summary: Imagine finding out that someone has been accessing your organization’s systems, stealing data, and moving between servers without anyone noticing. That’s the kind of situation organizations faced when ShinyHunters exploited a critical vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft. The attacks took place from May 27 to June 9, 2026, before Oracle issued its security alert. Universities were among the hardest hit, with some organizations suffering data breaches. How did the attackers get in, what should Oracle PeopleSoft users check, and what are the signs of compromise to look for? Who Are ShinyHunters? ShinyHunters is a cybercrime group that steals sensitive data and threatens to leak it unless victims pay. Instead of locking files with ransomware, it uses stolen data to pressure victims. ShinyHunters exploited a flaw to access PeopleSoft systems without logging in. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant linked the activity to UNC6240 [1] , which they track as ShinyHunters. According to Mandiant, the attacks began in late May 2026 and continued into June. The timing matters here. Oracle published its security alert on June 10 [2] , after the reported exploitation period. That means organizations could have been exposed before they had an official alert to act on. How Did the Attack on Oracle PeopleSoft Happen? CVE-2026-35273 affects Oracle PeopleTools 8.61 and 8.62 and has a critical CVSS score of 9.8. The problem lies in the Updates Environment Management component, which is associated with the Environment Management Hub and the PSEMHUB application. To put it simply, the vulnerable component fails to appropriately verify that an individual is authorized to access it. Without logging in, an attacker may be able to execute commands on the compromised system if they can connect to the endpoint via HTTP. Attackers can exploit the exposed endpoint remotely without stolen passwords or user interaction. On June 10, 2026, Oracle issued an alert, and on June 12, CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV Catalog [3] . Getting In Was Only the Beginning What happened after the initial access is just as important as the vulnerability itself. Mandiant’s investigation uncovered tools and scripts that showed how the attackers tried to maintain access, reach other systems, and steal information. Here’s what they found. 1. Remote access tools disguised as legitimate software The attackers deployed customized MeshCentral agents disguised as Microsoft Azure-related software. This gave them a way to access compromised systems remotely without relying on the original vulnerability every time. 2. Attempts to move across internal systems Investigators found a script designed to connect to other hosts over SSH using a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords. This is called lateral movement. Once attackers get into one system, they look for ways to reach other systems connected to it. 3. Data collection and theft Attackers sent stolen data to servers connected to ShinyHunters after compressing it. 4. Extortion using stolen information Data associated with the campaign later appeared on the group’s leak site. For affected organizations, that meant the incident wasn’t just about fixing a vulnerable server. Their sensitive information could also be exposed. Universities were hit particularly hard. Mandiant reported [4] notifying more than 100 organizations whose IP addresses matched potentially vulnerable endpoints. Around 68% were in higher education, most of them in the United States. Some organizations blocked the activity, while others were compromised. The University of Nottingham confirmed a cyberattack [5] . The exposed data could affect current and former students, with consequences beyond the university’s IT systems. How Can You Tell If ShinyHunters Have Been in Your Environment? Patching the vulnerability is important, but there’s another thing organizations need to check: did attackers get in before the fix was applied? That’s why security teams should look for signs of compromise rather than assuming the problem is solved once the vulnerable component is secured. Here are some things worth investigating: Suspicious requests: Check PeopleSoft and WebLogic logs for unexpected POST requests to /PSEMHUB/hub and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector. Unfamiliar JSP files: Look for unexpected files such as x.jsp, u.jsp, tunnel.jsp, and tunnel.jspx in the PSEMHUB.war directory. Unknown remote access tools: Investigate unfamiliar MeshCentral agents and executables disguised as legitimate software. Unusual SSH activity: Check for unexpected connections from PeopleSoft servers to other internal systems. Suspicious outbound traffic: Look for unusual data transfers and connections that could indicate data staging or exfiltration . There’s another detail to keep in mind. Attackers may use different URLs to bypass security tools. In September 2026, attackers used encoded paths like /%50SEMHUB/hub to bypass some WAF rules and reach the vulnerable endpoint. So, blocking the standard URL alone may not be enough. Security teams should also review how their WAF rules handle encoded paths. What Should You Do If You Use Oracle PeopleSoft? If you use PeopleSoft, check your PeopleTools version and whether the Environment Management Hub is exposed. Oracle recommends applying the appropriate security fixes. Its guidance also includes disabling the Environment Management Hub in multi-server configurations or removing the PSEMHUB application in single-server configurations, as applicable. If you can’t disable or remove the component immediately, restrict external access to /PSEMHUB/* and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector. You can find the official instructions in Oracle's security alert for CVE-2026-35273 . And don’t forget to check for signs of an earlier compromise. Check logs, suspicious files, and unusual connections. If you find anything, investigate whether attackers accessed other systems or stole data. The important thing is to address both problems: the vulnerability itself and any attacker who may already have used it. Why Visibility Matters After an Attack The ShinyHunters attack shows how attackers can gain access, spread to other systems, and steal data. That’s why security teams need to see more than the initial alert. They need to connect activity across networks, endpoints, and cloud environments to understand what happened and where an attacker may have gone next. Imagine finding out that someone has been accessing your organization’s systems, stealing data, and moving between servers without anyone noticing. That’s the kind of situation organizations faced when ShinyHunters exploited a critical vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft.

The attacks took place from May 27 to June 9, 2026, before Oracle issued its security alert. Universities were among the hardest hit, with some organizations suffering data breaches.

How did the attackers get in, what should Oracle PeopleSoft users check, and what are the signs of compromise to look for?

Who Are ShinyHunters?

ShinyHunters is a cybercrime group that steals sensitive data and threatens to leak it unless victims pay. Instead of locking files with ransomware, it uses stolen data to pressure victims.

ShinyHunters exploited a flaw to access PeopleSoft systems without logging in.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant linked the activity to UNC6240[1], which they track as ShinyHunters. According to Mandiant, the attacks began in late May 2026 and continued into June.

The timing matters here. Oracle published its security alert on June 10[2], after the reported exploitation period. That means organizations could have been exposed before they had an official alert to act on.

How Did the Attack on Oracle PeopleSoft Happen?

CVE-2026-35273 affects Oracle PeopleTools 8.61 and 8.62 and has a critical CVSS score of 9.8.

The problem lies in the Updates Environment Management component, which is associated with the Environment Management Hub and the PSEMHUB application.

To put it simply, the vulnerable component fails to appropriately verify that an individual is authorized to access it. Without logging in, an attacker may be able to execute commands on the compromised system if they can connect to the endpoint via HTTP.

Attackers can exploit the exposed endpoint remotely without stolen passwords or user interaction.

On June 10, 2026, Oracle issued an alert, and on June 12, CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV Catalog[3].

Getting In Was Only the Beginning

What happened after the initial access is just as important as the vulnerability itself.

Mandiant’s investigation uncovered tools and scripts that showed how the attackers tried to maintain access, reach other systems, and steal information.

Here’s what they found.

1. Remote access tools disguised as legitimate software

The attackers deployed customized MeshCentral agents disguised as Microsoft Azure-related software. This gave them a way to access compromised systems remotely without relying on the original vulnerability every time.

2. Attempts to move across internal systems

Investigators found a script designed to connect to other hosts over SSH using a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords. This is called lateral movement. Once attackers get into one system, they look for ways to reach other systems connected to it.

3. Data collection and theft

Attackers sent stolen data to servers connected to ShinyHunters after compressing it.

4. Extortion using stolen information

Data associated with the campaign later appeared on the group’s leak site. For affected organizations, that meant the incident wasn’t just about fixing a vulnerable server. Their sensitive information could also be exposed.

Universities were hit particularly hard. Mandiant reported[4] notifying more than 100 organizations whose IP addresses matched potentially vulnerable endpoints. Around 68% were in higher education, most of them in the United States. Some organizations blocked the activity, while others were compromised.

The University of Nottingham confirmed a cyberattack[5]. The exposed data could affect current and former students, with consequences beyond the university’s IT systems.

How Can You Tell If ShinyHunters Have Been in Your Environment?

Patching the vulnerability is important, but there’s another thing organizations need to check: did attackers get in before the fix was applied?

That’s why security teams should look for signs of compromise rather than assuming the problem is solved once the vulnerable component is secured.

Here are some things worth investigating:

  • Suspicious requests:
    Check PeopleSoft and WebLogic logs for unexpected POST requests to /PSEMHUB/hub and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector.
  • Unfamiliar JSP files:
    Look for unexpected files such as x.jsp, u.jsp, tunnel.jsp, and tunnel.jspx in the PSEMHUB.war directory.
  • Unknown remote access tools:
    Investigate unfamiliar MeshCentral agents and executables disguised as legitimate software.
  • Unusual SSH activity:
    Check for unexpected connections from PeopleSoft servers to other internal systems.
  • Suspicious outbound traffic:
    Look for unusual data transfers and connections that could indicate data staging or exfiltration.

There’s another detail to keep in mind. Attackers may use different URLs to bypass security tools.

In September 2026, attackers used encoded paths like /%50SEMHUB/hub to bypass some WAF rules and reach the vulnerable endpoint.

So, blocking the standard URL alone may not be enough. Security teams should also review how their WAF rules handle encoded paths.

What Should You Do If You Use Oracle PeopleSoft?

If you use PeopleSoft, check your PeopleTools version and whether the Environment Management Hub is exposed.

Oracle recommends applying the appropriate security fixes. Its guidance also includes disabling the Environment Management Hub in multi-server configurations or removing the PSEMHUB application in single-server configurations, as applicable.

If you can’t disable or remove the component immediately, restrict external access to /PSEMHUB/* and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector.

  • You can find the official instructions in Oracle's security alert for CVE-2026-35273.

And don’t forget to check for signs of an earlier compromise. Check logs, suspicious files, and unusual connections. If you find anything, investigate whether attackers accessed other systems or stole data.

The important thing is to address both problems: the vulnerability itself and any attacker who may already have used it.

Why Visibility Matters After an Attack

The ShinyHunters attack shows how attackers can gain access, spread to other systems, and steal data.

That’s why security teams need to see more than the initial alert. They need to connect activity across networks, endpoints, and cloud environments to understand what happened and where an attacker may have gone next.

The technopolitics of ad-tech ( permalink ) "Technopolitics" are the politics embedded in technology. The Ur-text of technopolitics is "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" by the rock critic turned scholar Langdon Winner: https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf With "Do Artifacts," Winner demands that we move beyond the idea of technologies having "intended consequences" and "unintended consequences" and towards a political economy of tech. In service to this, he divides the politics of artifacts into three categories: I. Artifacts that have politics embedded in them by their creators, like Robert Moses's infamous bridges over the Long Island parkways. According to Moses biographer Robert Caro, Moses deliberately specified that these bridges must be too low for a city bus to pass under, in a bid to block Black people from traveling from New York City to the beaches he'd developed on Long Island. Today those bridges are more than a century old, and they are still too low for city buses to pass under them, and this continues to mean that people who don't own private vehicles find it more difficult to get to the beach, and as it's still the case that race is a predictor of low incomes, those are still racist bridges. II. Artifacts whose politics are accidental but unavoidable. Winner cites a kind of tomato harvester that vastly improved the efficiency of tomato pickers. These harvesters became very popular, which allowed tomato farmers to lay off large numbers of agricultural workers, and also allowed them to price the mechanically harvested tomatoes so cheaply that they crowded out other kinds of tomatoes. Because these machines created a large pool of unemployed workers, they shifted power from labor to capital, and because these picking machines were too rough for all but the hardest varietals of tomato, they changed the flavor profile of tomatoes in America for the worse, towards a bland, tough tomato. These picking machines were not designed to make workers poorer, nor were they designed to make tomatoes taste worse, but because of their technical characteristics, this was the unavoidable outcome, the inextricable politics of these machines. III. Artifacts whose politics are intrinsic to their design. Here, Winner contrasts solar panels with nuclear reactors. Solar panels may require highly centralized industrial systems to produce , but once they are in the field, solar panels are compatible with looser, less coordinated political arrangements. A world of small anarchist communes is fully compatible with solar energy. Contrast this with nuclear reactors: the prudent ongoing operation of a reactor requires a highly centralized state that is capable of fielding reliable, trustworthy independent inspectors. This state must also be capable of exercising the coercive power to shut down badly maintained or incompetently operated reactors. The politics of nukes are the politics of a centralized, powerful state; the politics of solar are less determined. Solar is compatible with a wide variety of political systems, including (but not limited to) weak, decentralized states. (For a further exploration of "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" I highly recommend Ginger Coons' reading guide:) https://www.not-so-obvious.net/reading-do-artifacts-have-politics/ I really like Winner's framework for exploring technopolitics, but I have my own gloss on it. Winner's framework doesn't explicitly contemplate the idea of technological countermeasures . For example, what if someone were to design a city bus that was low enough to fit under Robert Moses's bridges? At that point, they'd cease to be "racist bridges," and merely become "bridges built by a racist": https://locusmag.com/feature/commentary-cory-doctorow-technopolitics/ Which brings me to the technopolitics of ad-tech. Lots of people think that advertising is "the original sin of the internet," setting in motion the surveillance dystopia that is closing in on us from all sides today: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/17/mercenary-spyware/#discover-tech I think this is wrong. I think that finding ways to communicate ideas and pitches to the general public is fine. Without some channel for reaching people with ideas and propositions they may not be familiar with, it would be infinitely harder to reach people for political causes. It would also be harder for new books, movies and music to find new audiences. It would be much harder to get people out to your independent craft fair, your zine show, or your No Kings march. For me, the internet's original sin isn't advertising , it's surveillance . Contrary to what you have been told – and pax Winner's framework – the internet is fully compatible with privacy: https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/31/losing-the-crypto-wars/#surveillance-monopolism It wasn't the internet's technopolitics that made it a surveillance nightmare. It was just plain politics . Specifically, our politicians decided to stop enacting and enforcing privacy laws. The last consumer privacy law we got in America was a bill that made it illegal for video store clerks to disclose your VHS rentals: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Privacy_Protection_Act (As I type these words, the Supreme Court is poised to eliminate even that dried-up old crumb of privacy protection:) https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2026/10/supreme-court-privacy-rights-case-bork-kavanaugh.html The widespread phenomenon of ad-tech companies spying on us is the result of the decision to allow them to do so . That decision has had innumerable negative downstream effects, such as skyrocketing "surveillance prices": https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/11/nothing-personal/#instacartography And collapsing "surveillance wages": https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point It's created vast surveillance databases that are critical to Trump's racist pogroms, providing dossiers and precise location data on the people ICE kidnaps to Salvadoran slave-labor camps: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes Surveillance also promotes oligarchy. Without surveillance, oligarchs must give up more of their fortunes to keep the public happy, because the alternative is spending even more money on guards to keep the public from building guillotines on their lawns. Surveillance lets oligarchs make targeted strikes on restive radicals, which is much cheaper than broad-spectrum policies that make us all better off and neutralize the case for guillotines: https://pluralistic.net/2025/06/26/autostabilizer/#slicey-bois These are the technopolitics of surveillance , not advertising. There is nothing about advertising that demands surveillance. For centuries, advertising was not meaningfully linked to surveillance. The decision to fuse surveillance with advertising was just that – a decision , not an inevitability. Any time we forget this, we let spying tech bosses off the hook. After all, if advertising demands surveillance, then tech bosses are just the avatars of the great forces of history, prisoners of the imperative to spy in order to advertise. By remembering that surveillance advertising is a choice , we put the blame squarely where it belongs: on the guillotineable oligarchs who made that choice, and amassed spectacular fortunes thereby. Surveillance is political, but surveillance advertising has its own distinct technopolitics, and to understand those technopolitics, we must contrast them with the technopolitics of contextual advertising . Up until a decade or two ago, contextual advertising was simply called "advertising." Contextual advertising is the practice of running refrigerator ads next to articles on cooking and kitchen remodeling; ads for roadside restaurants on highway billboards; ads for Disney vacations in parenting magazines. Your intuition probably insists that context advertising is less effective than surveillance advertising. After all, surveillance advertising allows a running shoe company to target users who are training for a marathon no matter where they are and no matter what they're doing. Surely this translates into increased "conversions" (clicks and/or purchases, depending on who you're talking to)? It does, but not by much. Advertisers get about 5% more value from surveillance ads than they do from context ads: https://weis2019.econinfosec.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2019/05/WEIS_2019_paper_38.pdf Partly, that's because surveillance ad companies grossly overrate the efficacy of surveillance advertising: https://peoples-things.ghost.io/youre-doing-it-wrong-notes-on-criticism-and-technology-hype/ But surveillance advertising's anemic returns to advertisers are down to another aspect of the system: its tendency towards monopolization: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Google_LLC_(2023) Surveillance is a capital-intensive activity: spying on billions of people as they move through the digital and physical world is incredibly expensive. That is a good part of the reason that online advertising has collapsed into the Meta/Google duopoly, who control about 80% of display advertising. The harms of surveillance monopolies have a severely distorting effect on policy debates. For example, it's led some anti-monopolists to call for government-issued surveillance identifiers that follow us from birth to death in order to facilitate commercial spying to foster more competition in surveillance: https://www.thesling.org/what-to-do-about-googles-dominance-of-online-advertising/ Here's the thing about monopolists: they cheat. Google and Meta have an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the advertising market, overcharging advertisers and underpaying publishers: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue The ad-tech giants have taken in hundreds of billions that they simply can't account for. It's disappeared down a fraud-hole: https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/25/lying-spies/#spying-liars All of this has driven the majority of web users to install a privacy-blocker (like EFF's Privacybadger.org), meaning that surveillance ads are disproportionately likely to not even show up in a reader's browser: https://doc.searls.com/2023/11/11/how-is-the-worlds-biggest-boycott-doing/ So while it's possible that, in a state of nature, a surveillance ad would outperform a context ad, delivering more sales for advertisers and more revenue for publishers, the monopolistic tendency of ad-tech means that publishers earn less from surveillance ads (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher commissions), and advertisers see fewer sales from them (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher prices). Context ads, meanwhile, are always going to give power to publishers, because publishers will always understand the materials they publish better than any ad-tech platform could. Commissioning, editing and publishing an article, podcast or video gives a publisher unique and inalienable insight into that material. Surveillance data about audiences is a kind of ambient vapor floating around websites and places and payments that has to be condensed through a heroic and expensive effort that gives power to whichever company can muster the capital and infrastructure to do so. Meanwhile, information about the content of publishers' offerings is already refined into ingots that are already in publishers' own possession. It's possible to run "programmatic ads" without surveillance. Rather than building an ad-tech stack through which publishers transmit sensitive information about their audiences ("Who will pay me to advertise to this 18-34 year old man-child from the outer boroughs who owns an Xbox and has recently researched gonorrhea symptoms?"), we can build systems through which publishers transmit information about their own materials ("Who will advertise to a user with a New York IP address who is reading an article comparing running shoe brands?"). Not only is this possible, but it actually generates more revenues for publishers than the surveillance-based ad-tech stack: https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/24/data-from-dutch-public-broadcaster-shows-the-value-of-ditching-creepy-ads/ On top of that, publishers who don't gather personal information about users also don't need to show their users those awful pop-up ads asking their permission to gather their data. Everyone hates those notices, and they are yet another negative aspect of surveillance advertising that disappears with the switch to context ads. An ad-tech stack for context ads is far less prone to monopolization. Such a stack can be "federated," with multiple "demand-side platforms" (the part of the system that advertisers use to place bids for the right to show their ads) all communicating with the same "supply-side platform" (the part of the system publishers use to transmit opportunities to place ads). This is also in the technopolitics of context ads: they do not tend toward the "efficiencies of scale" that lead to abusive monopolistic middlemen who steal from publishers and advertisers and sell out the public to fascists who want to arrest them and deport them to Salvadoran slave-labor camps. When the ad-tech sector is composed of smaller companies that are more competitive with one another, it is much harder for any of them to collude to rig the market. That fierce competition also means it's harder to create a cozy conspiracy to lobby together to block privacy laws, and it leaves the companies with lower margins and less retained earnings to spend on those lobbying efforts. Surveillance ads also promote all kinds of parasitic businesses. The fact that a publisher can serve ads related to users rather than the subject of their media means that sensationalistic and deceptive websites can sell ads that run against content that's totally unrelated to advertisers' products and services. And because it's cheaper to produce lies and garbage, these publishers can undercut the ad prices demanded by high quality outlets and let advertisers reach the same users. This is the whole reason that "chumboxes" exist: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chumbox Just as nuclear power favors a centralized state, surveillance advertising: favors middlemen over publishers and advertisers; tends toward monopoly; favors low-quality media over high-quality production; impedes the passage of privacy laws; provides authoritarian states with an off-the-books, warrantless source of surveillance data. And just as solar allows for decentralized, anti-authoritarian societies, context advertising: favors publishers over middlemen and advertisers; tends towards pluralism and diversity of voices; favors high-quality media by reserving the lion's share of the rewards to the producers; does not rely on a weak privacy environment; does not militate for "democratizing spying" by issuing every person with a permanent advertising identifier. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with building systems to tell people about things you want them to know. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with paying for media with ads. It's possible for both of these things to go awry, but they are not in and of themselves bad. They have contingent technopolitics. But surveillance ads have completely unavoidable, absolutely ghastly technopolitics. Surveillance ads are bad for publishers, for advertisers, and for democracy. The technopolitics of ad-tech (permalink)

"Technopolitics" are the politics embedded in technology. The Ur-text of technopolitics is "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" by the rock critic turned scholar Langdon Winner:

https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf

With "Do Artifacts," Winner demands that we move beyond the idea of technologies having "intended consequences" and "unintended consequences" and towards a political economy of tech. In service to this, he divides the politics of artifacts into three categories:

I. Artifacts that have politics embedded in them by their creators, like Robert Moses's infamous bridges over the Long Island parkways. According to Moses biographer Robert Caro, Moses deliberately specified that these bridges must be too low for a city bus to pass under, in a bid to block Black people from traveling from New York City to the beaches he'd developed on Long Island.

Today those bridges are more than a century old, and they are still too low for city buses to pass under them, and this continues to mean that people who don't own private vehicles find it more difficult to get to the beach, and as it's still the case that race is a predictor of low incomes, those are still racist bridges.

II. Artifacts whose politics are accidental but unavoidable. Winner cites a kind of tomato harvester that vastly improved the efficiency of tomato pickers. These harvesters became very popular, which allowed tomato farmers to lay off large numbers of agricultural workers, and also allowed them to price the mechanically harvested tomatoes so cheaply that they crowded out other kinds of tomatoes.

Because these machines created a large pool of unemployed workers, they shifted power from labor to capital, and because these picking machines were too rough for all but the hardest varietals of tomato, they changed the flavor profile of tomatoes in America for the worse, towards a bland, tough tomato.

These picking machines were not designed to make workers poorer, nor were they designed to make tomatoes taste worse, but because of their technical characteristics, this was the unavoidable outcome, the inextricable politics of these machines.

III. Artifacts whose politics are intrinsic to their design. Here, Winner contrasts solar panels with nuclear reactors. Solar panels may require highly centralized industrial systems to produce, but once they are in the field, solar panels are compatible with looser, less coordinated political arrangements. A world of small anarchist communes is fully compatible with solar energy.

Contrast this with nuclear reactors: the prudent ongoing operation of a reactor requires a highly centralized state that is capable of fielding reliable, trustworthy independent inspectors. This state must also be capable of exercising the coercive power to shut down badly maintained or incompetently operated reactors.

The politics of nukes are the politics of a centralized, powerful state; the politics of solar are less determined. Solar is compatible with a wide variety of political systems, including (but not limited to) weak, decentralized states.

(For a further exploration of "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" I highly recommend Ginger Coons' reading guide:)

https://www.not-so-obvious.net/reading-do-artifacts-have-politics/

I really like Winner's framework for exploring technopolitics, but I have my own gloss on it. Winner's framework doesn't explicitly contemplate the idea of technological countermeasures. For example, what if someone were to design a city bus that was low enough to fit under Robert Moses's bridges? At that point, they'd cease to be "racist bridges," and merely become "bridges built by a racist":

https://locusmag.com/feature/commentary-cory-doctorow-technopolitics/

Which brings me to the technopolitics of ad-tech. Lots of people think that advertising is "the original sin of the internet," setting in motion the surveillance dystopia that is closing in on us from all sides today:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/17/mercenary-spyware/#discover-tech

I think this is wrong. I think that finding ways to communicate ideas and pitches to the general public is fine. Without some channel for reaching people with ideas and propositions they may not be familiar with, it would be infinitely harder to reach people for political causes. It would also be harder for new books, movies and music to find new audiences. It would be much harder to get people out to your independent craft fair, your zine show, or your No Kings march.

For me, the internet's original sin isn't advertising, it's surveillance. Contrary to what you have been told – and pax Winner's framework – the internet is fully compatible with privacy:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/31/losing-the-crypto-wars/#surveillance-monopolism

It wasn't the internet's technopolitics that made it a surveillance nightmare. It was just plain politics. Specifically, our politicians decided to stop enacting and enforcing privacy laws. The last consumer privacy law we got in America was a bill that made it illegal for video store clerks to disclose your VHS rentals:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Privacy_Protection_Act

(As I type these words, the Supreme Court is poised to eliminate even that dried-up old crumb of privacy protection:)

https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2026/10/supreme-court-privacy-rights-case-bork-kavanaugh.html

The widespread phenomenon of ad-tech companies spying on us is the result of the decision to allow them to do so. That decision has had innumerable negative downstream effects, such as skyrocketing "surveillance prices":

https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/11/nothing-personal/#instacartography

And collapsing "surveillance wages":

https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point

It's created vast surveillance databases that are critical to Trump's racist pogroms, providing dossiers and precise location data on the people ICE kidnaps to Salvadoran slave-labor camps:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes

Surveillance also promotes oligarchy. Without surveillance, oligarchs must give up more of their fortunes to keep the public happy, because the alternative is spending even more money on guards to keep the public from building guillotines on their lawns. Surveillance lets oligarchs make targeted strikes on restive radicals, which is much cheaper than broad-spectrum policies that make us all better off and neutralize the case for guillotines:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/06/26/autostabilizer/#slicey-bois

These are the technopolitics of surveillance, not advertising. There is nothing about advertising that demands surveillance. For centuries, advertising was not meaningfully linked to surveillance. The decision to fuse surveillance with advertising was just that – a decision, not an inevitability.

Any time we forget this, we let spying tech bosses off the hook. After all, if advertising demands surveillance, then tech bosses are just the avatars of the great forces of history, prisoners of the imperative to spy in order to advertise. By remembering that surveillance advertising is a choice, we put the blame squarely where it belongs: on the guillotineable oligarchs who made that choice, and amassed spectacular fortunes thereby.

Surveillance is political, but surveillance advertising has its own distinct technopolitics, and to understand those technopolitics, we must contrast them with the technopolitics of contextual advertising. Up until a decade or two ago, contextual advertising was simply called "advertising." Contextual advertising is the practice of running refrigerator ads next to articles on cooking and kitchen remodeling; ads for roadside restaurants on highway billboards; ads for Disney vacations in parenting magazines.

Your intuition probably insists that context advertising is less effective than surveillance advertising. After all, surveillance advertising allows a running shoe company to target users who are training for a marathon no matter where they are and no matter what they're doing. Surely this translates into increased "conversions" (clicks and/or purchases, depending on who you're talking to)?

It does, but not by much. Advertisers get about 5% more value from surveillance ads than they do from context ads:

https://weis2019.econinfosec.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2019/05/WEIS_2019_paper_38.pdf

Partly, that's because surveillance ad companies grossly overrate the efficacy of surveillance advertising:

https://peoples-things.ghost.io/youre-doing-it-wrong-notes-on-criticism-and-technology-hype/

But surveillance advertising's anemic returns to advertisers are down to another aspect of the system: its tendency towards monopolization:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Google_LLC_(2023)

Surveillance is a capital-intensive activity: spying on billions of people as they move through the digital and physical world is incredibly expensive. That is a good part of the reason that online advertising has collapsed into the Meta/Google duopoly, who control about 80% of display advertising.

The harms of surveillance monopolies have a severely distorting effect on policy debates. For example, it's led some anti-monopolists to call for government-issued surveillance identifiers that follow us from birth to death in order to facilitate commercial spying to foster more competition in surveillance:

https://www.thesling.org/what-to-do-about-googles-dominance-of-online-advertising/

Here's the thing about monopolists: they cheat. Google and Meta have an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the advertising market, overcharging advertisers and underpaying publishers:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue

The ad-tech giants have taken in hundreds of billions that they simply can't account for. It's disappeared down a fraud-hole:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/25/lying-spies/#spying-liars

All of this has driven the majority of web users to install a privacy-blocker (like EFF's Privacybadger.org), meaning that surveillance ads are disproportionately likely to not even show up in a reader's browser:

https://doc.searls.com/2023/11/11/how-is-the-worlds-biggest-boycott-doing/

So while it's possible that, in a state of nature, a surveillance ad would outperform a context ad, delivering more sales for advertisers and more revenue for publishers, the monopolistic tendency of ad-tech means that publishers earn less from surveillance ads (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher commissions), and advertisers see fewer sales from them (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher prices).

Context ads, meanwhile, are always going to give power to publishers, because publishers will always understand the materials they publish better than any ad-tech platform could. Commissioning, editing and publishing an article, podcast or video gives a publisher unique and inalienable insight into that material.

Surveillance data about audiences is a kind of ambient vapor floating around websites and places and payments that has to be condensed through a heroic and expensive effort that gives power to whichever company can muster the capital and infrastructure to do so. Meanwhile, information about the content of publishers' offerings is already refined into ingots that are already in publishers' own possession.

It's possible to run "programmatic ads" without surveillance. Rather than building an ad-tech stack through which publishers transmit sensitive information about their audiences ("Who will pay me to advertise to this 18-34 year old man-child from the outer boroughs who owns an Xbox and has recently researched gonorrhea symptoms?"), we can build systems through which publishers transmit information about their own materials ("Who will advertise to a user with a New York IP address who is reading an article comparing running shoe brands?").

Not only is this possible, but it actually generates more revenues for publishers than the surveillance-based ad-tech stack:

https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/24/data-from-dutch-public-broadcaster-shows-the-value-of-ditching-creepy-ads/

On top of that, publishers who don't gather personal information about users also don't need to show their users those awful pop-up ads asking their permission to gather their data. Everyone hates those notices, and they are yet another negative aspect of surveillance advertising that disappears with the switch to context ads.

An ad-tech stack for context ads is far less prone to monopolization. Such a stack can be "federated," with multiple "demand-side platforms" (the part of the system that advertisers use to place bids for the right to show their ads) all communicating with the same "supply-side platform" (the part of the system publishers use to transmit opportunities to place ads).

This is also in the technopolitics of context ads: they do not tend toward the "efficiencies of scale" that lead to abusive monopolistic middlemen who steal from publishers and advertisers and sell out the public to fascists who want to arrest them and deport them to Salvadoran slave-labor camps.

When the ad-tech sector is composed of smaller companies that are more competitive with one another, it is much harder for any of them to collude to rig the market. That fierce competition also means it's harder to create a cozy conspiracy to lobby together to block privacy laws, and it leaves the companies with lower margins and less retained earnings to spend on those lobbying efforts.

Surveillance ads also promote all kinds of parasitic businesses. The fact that a publisher can serve ads related to users rather than the subject of their media means that sensationalistic and deceptive websites can sell ads that run against content that's totally unrelated to advertisers' products and services. And because it's cheaper to produce lies and garbage, these publishers can undercut the ad prices demanded by high quality outlets and let advertisers reach the same users. This is the whole reason that "chumboxes" exist:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chumbox

Just as nuclear power favors a centralized state, surveillance advertising:

  • favors middlemen over publishers and advertisers;

  • tends toward monopoly;

  • favors low-quality media over high-quality production;

  • impedes the passage of privacy laws;

  • provides authoritarian states with an off-the-books, warrantless source of surveillance data.

And just as solar allows for decentralized, anti-authoritarian societies, context advertising:

  • favors publishers over middlemen and advertisers;

  • tends towards pluralism and diversity of voices;

  • favors high-quality media by reserving the lion's share of the rewards to the producers;

  • does not rely on a weak privacy environment;

  • does not militate for "democratizing spying" by issuing every person with a permanent advertising identifier.

There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with building systems to tell people about things you want them to know. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with paying for media with ads. It's possible for both of these things to go awry, but they are not in and of themselves bad. They have contingent technopolitics.

But surveillance ads have completely unavoidable, absolutely ghastly technopolitics. Surveillance ads are bad for publishers, for advertisers, and for democracy. We should ban surveillance ads:

https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/05/save-news-we-must-ban-surveillance-advertising

items.title: Google Unveils New Android AI Protections to Block Scam Calls, Phishing Links and OTP Theft
items.summary: Google has announced a new set of Android security protections designed to stop mobile scams across calls, text messages, chat apps, web links, and account verification codes. The update comes as criminals increasingly use spoofed phone numbers, fake bank alerts, phishing pages, remote screen sharing, and AI-generated voices to trick users into giving up money or login details. Google said its existing AI-powered scam detection tools in Phone by Google and Google Messages already identify more than five million suspected scam calls and texts each month. The new protections focus on preventing users from reaching the most dangerous stage of a scam. Instead of only blocking known malicious links or spam numbers. Android will use a mix of on-device AI, cloud-based analysis, privacy protections, and real-time checks to identify suspicious behavior before victims share passwords, payment data, or one-time passcodes. A key addition is an opt-in Enhanced Protection mode in Google Messages. Google said the setting will roll out in the coming weeks and will activate stronger protections for complex messaging scams. multi-layered protections across Google Messages (Source: Google) This includes expanded Scam Detection using Google’s Private AI Compute platform, which allows Gemini models to review the context of a conversation with an unknown sender. Google Unveils New Android AI Protections The aim is to spot slow-moving social engineering scams where criminals build trust over several messages before sending a fraudulent request or link. Google said the analysis occurs in an encrypted environment that Google employees cannot access. Enhanced Protection will also strengthen link checks in Google Messages. Scammers frequently create new phishing domains that have not yet been added to threat blocklists, which can make standard URL filtering less effective. Google said Gemini Nano, its on-device AI model, will combine real-time web signals with local analysis to assess unfamiliar links before a user opens them. Scam Detection in chat notifications (Source: Google) Android will also show redesigned warnings for links from numbers not saved in the user’s contacts. This provides an extra checkpoint before users visit a potential phishing page. The company is also expanding scam alerts from Pixel devices to a wider Android ecosystem. Scam Detection in chat notifications can flag suspicious messages from supported chat apps directly in the notification panel, allowing users to see a warning before opening the message. Google is working with Android device makers to bring the on-device feature to hundreds of millions of additional users later this year. Google’s update also targets phone-based social engineering scams, particularly cases where criminals persuade victims to share their screen or redirect incoming calls. Android will now automatically hide login fields and payment screens during active screen-sharing sessions in Chrome and Android WebView. The Protection is designed to stop fraudsters from viewing passwords, card details, and other sensitive information while guiding a victim through a fake support or banking process. Proactive call-forwarding protection (Source: Google) Another major safeguard addresses OTP theft through call forwarding . Threat actors may trick a user into entering a call-forwarding code, redirecting incoming calls containing verification codes to a criminal-controlled number. Android will block apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warn users before a manually entered MMI forwarding code takes effect. Security teams can also review related account takeover risks and prevention steps in Cyber Security News coverage of OTP bypass and MFA phishing campaigns and mobile banking malware . Google is also expanding verified financial calls, a feature built with banks including Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco. The system checks whether the bank’s official app actually initiated a call claiming to come from a bank. Built-in scam defenses across Android and iOS (Source: Google) If verification fails, Android can end the call and alert the user. Google said the feature has blocked more than three million spoofed calls involving the two Brazilian banks since its June launch. The announcement shows mobile security shifting from simple spam filtering to behavior-based fraud prevention. Users should still avoid sharing passwords, card information, recovery codes, or OTPs over calls and messages, even when the caller appears legitimate. items.summary: Hackers are exploiting flaws in Plex Media Server to install cryptocurrency mining malware, with a researcher recording successful attacks against a honeypot on October 17, 2026. The activity follows the release of Plex2Shell, a public exploit that chains four vulnerabilities to run code without logging in. Later observations also revealed proxy software running alongside the miner. The findings from Boredhackerblog show active exploitation of an exposed test server, rather than scanning alone. The researcher also warned that restrictions on outbound traffic initially prevented collection of some payloads. Its official security notice warned that NAS users might need to install updates manually. Cyber Security News previously covered the Plex security update and affected releases . The exploit combines CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. According to the Plex2Shell repository , the chain starts with server-side request forgery, which tricks Plex into sending requests chosen by an attacker. It then reaches internal functions, gains access to owner-authorized requests, and writes a file to an attacker-selected location. The final stage abuses the loading of an unsigned codec to execute code. The repository identifies versions before 1.43.3.10828 as vulnerable and lists 1.43.3.10861 as fixed. Although the exploit supports Linux and Windows targets, the reported honeypot activity involved a Linux-based Plex deployment running in Docker. items.title: Microsoft Confirms October Windows Updates Can Break Exchange Server Email Services
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that Windows Server security updates released on October 13, 2026, can disrupt Exchange Server email services, blocking webmail access and leaving messages undelivered. The issue affects some on-premises systems running Exchange Server 2016, Exchange Server 2019, and Exchange Server Subscription Edition. Microsoft has published a workaround and advises administrators not to uninstall the Windows updates. The failures stem from changes in Windows Server, not the separate October Exchange Server security updates. Servers can experience problems even without installing the latest Exchange patches, making the underlying operating system update the key factor when investigating these outages. Affected Updates and Exchange Server Symptoms Microsoft identified four Windows updates linked to the failures. These are KB5126646 for Windows Server 2025, KB5126655 for Windows Server 2022, KB5126651 for Windows Server 2019, and KB5126868 for Windows Server 2016. The impact depends on server workload, and some systems may never develop symptoms. Users may be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web, while messages sent through Outlook remain stuck in the Outbox. Administrators may notice growing mail queues, failed mailbox access during replication, or problems with Database Availability Group members reaching quorum. Restarting an affected server may restore service temporarily. One error administrators should watch for is MapiExceptionMdbOffline: Unable to make connection to the server. (hr=0x80004005, ec=1142) . Affected systems may also record Event ID 1006 in the Application log, providing a useful sign when checking whether an outage matches Microsoft’s report. According to Microsoft’s Windows release health notice , the October updates introduced a default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls. This limit controls memory use by Endpoint Mapper, a Windows component involved in remote procedure call communications. Heavy Exchange workloads can exceed the default allowance. Increasing the limit allows Endpoint Mapper to use more memory to handle these calls. Microsoft currently lists the issue as mitigated rather than resolved and says its investigation remains ongoing. An additional mitigation is available through Microsoft Support for affected organizations. Microsoft’s Registry Workaround Microsoft’s Exchange Team advisory instructs administrators to open an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange server and run reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f . The server must then be restarted. After the reboot, administrators should monitor the environment for recurring failures. Following earlier reporting on out-of-support Exchange servers , Microsoft says October 2026 marks their last scheduled ESU security release, with future updates limited to Subscription Edition.
